The labels

Florence, October. The exhibition "The Madonna with two faces" opens in three days at the Biblioteca delle Oblate. Chiara has asked Pietro to write the labels for the works. Pietro has brought her the first text.
I wrote: "This is the panel. The panel is fourteenth-century. On the panel there is the Madonna."
Three sentences, three times "panel". Join them with a relative: "The panel, on which the Madonna is painted, is fourteenth-century."
"Sulla quale"? Can't you say "su cui"?
You can. But in a label "il quale" sounds more elegant. And you understand at once what it refers to: "la quale" is feminine, singular.
And for the painter? "The painter is anonymous. The painter's name isn't known."
"The painter, whose name remains unknown…" Il cui: the painter's name.
And the hand pointing down? I want to say it makes you think of a donor, but without repeating everything.
Use "il che": "The Madonna points downwards, which suggests a donor." "Il che" picks up the whole previous sentence.
And at the end I want to write a sentence for the visitors. "People who look carefully see the hand."
Shorter: "Whoever looks carefully sees the hand." "Chi" means "the person who". It's the most beautiful sentence in the exhibition.

"Il cui" = whose. The article agrees with the thing possessed, not with the possessor:

"Il pittore, la cui mano" — "la" because "mano" is feminine, even though the painter is a man. As in Romanian: "pictorul, a cărui mână".
3. Il che: which
"Il che" picks up an idea or a whole sentence, not a word:
La Madonna indica in basso, il che fa pensare a un donatore.
The Madonna points downwards, which makes you think of a donor.
La predella è perduta, il che complica tutto.

Sono venute trecento persone, del che siamo felici.

In speech you can also say "e questo": "La predella è perduta, e questo complica tutto." "Il che" is more elegant, suited to written texts.

Il Maestro della Mano

The exhibition was called "The Madonna with two faces" and occupied the exhibition hall of the Biblioteca delle Oblate, the same one in which, two years earlier, Pietro had won the debate tournament. It was a small exhibition: a single room, six panels, two works. But it was the exhibition the diocese had insisted on in its negotiation with the cooperative, the one for which Monsignor Cappelli had given up a thousand euros. The eighteenth-century Madonna, which the parishioners had lent for six weeks after a long assembly, would be displayed in the centre of the room. Next to her, the digital reconstruction of the fourteenth-century Madonna, printed life-size. Around them, the panels with the analyses, the infrared photographs, the 1709 register and Davide's drawings. The curators were Chiara and Karl. The labels, by Chiara's decision, would be written by Pietro.

"Why me?" Pietro had asked, when Chiara suggested it. "Because you know how to explain things to people who know nothing about them," she had replied. "Karl and I know too much. We'd write labels only restorers would understand." So, for two weeks, Pietro wrote and rewrote. It was harder than he thought. A label had to be short, clear, precise, and at the same time make you want to look. The first versions were full of short sentences and repetitions: "This is the panel. The panel is poplar. The poplar was felled in the fourteenth century." Chiara read them with a red pencil in her hand and taught him to join sentences with relatives, the way the pieces of a mosaic are joined. "Il quale, la quale, il cui, il che," she told him. "They're the glue of elegant sentences."

To practise, Pietro began using relatives everywhere, even where they weren't needed. One evening, at the trattoria, he offered to rewrite the menu by hand, on the blackboard next to the door. When Graziella came out of the kitchen, she found written: "Ribollita, whose recipe is secret. Pappa al pomodoro, which means bread and tomato, but better. Steak, for which it is advisable to be hungry. Tiramisù, for which the cook takes no responsibility." The customers laughed and photographed the blackboard. Two Japanese tourists asked whether it was a poem. Graziella read it with her hands on her hips, in silence, and Pietro thought she would kill him. Instead she took the chalk and added a single line at the bottom: "Whoever criticises the menu washes the dishes." Then she went back into the kitchen. The blackboard stayed like that for three weeks, and Mancini published it on the Sunday page under the headline: "Grammar comes to the trattoria".

The biggest problem was the fourteenth-century painter. He had no name. Pietro didn't know what to call him on the labels. "The unknown author" seemed sad to him. "A Sienese painter" seemed vague. It was Karl who explained the solution art historians have used for over a century. When an old painter is anonymous but his works are recognisable, he is given a conventional name: the name of a famous work, or of the place where it is. So there is the Master of the Magdalen, the Master of the Osservanza, the Master of Figline. "And so ours," said Karl, "is the Master of San Leonardo. At least until someone finds his real name." Pietro thought for a moment. "It's like a nickname," he said. "Like Lupino for Grandma's dog." Karl laughed. "More or less," he said. "But with more dignity."

The transport of the eighteenth-century Madonna from San Leonardo to Florence was a small event. On the morning of departure, in front of the church, there were more than forty parishioners, who had come to say goodbye to her as you say goodbye to a relative leaving on a long journey. Karl and Chiara packed her in a special crate, with a small device inside measuring humidity and temperature during the journey, to prevent the wood from suffering. Don Paolo blessed the van. Signora Nunzia, leaning on her stick, touched the crate with her hand, as you touch someone's shoulder, and said in a low voice: "Come back soon. And let them look at you properly." The van set off at walking pace along the dirt road, followed for about a hundred metres by a group of children on bicycles. In Florence, on arrival, the device still showed the same humidity as the church. Karl showed it to everyone proudly, like a trophy.

The main label, the one that would hang next to the reconstruction, Pietro rewrote eleven times. The final version, which Chiara approved without changing a word, read: "Master of San Leonardo, active in Siena around 1320–1340. Madonna and Child. Digital reconstruction. The panel, on which the painter painted this Madonna, was cut from a poplar between 1318 and 1330. The work, whose original colours have been reconstructed thanks to the analyses, was badly damaged by a fire in 1709, which explains why an eighteenth-century painter covered it over. The Madonna looks at whoever comes in and points with her hand at a spot below, outside the picture. What she is pointing at, nobody knows yet. Whoever looks carefully will perhaps find out."

Davide, meanwhile, had finished his book. It was called "The diary of a tree", like the sentence Pietro had said to Dr Lapini, and told the story of the Madonna from the point of view of the poplar from which the panel had been cut. The poplar was born in a valley near Siena in 1210, grew for a hundred years, was felled, became a panel, was painted, burned, was covered over, waited three hundred years under another painting, and in the end was "looked at by a boy who asked too many questions". It was forty pages of watercolours, with a few handwritten sentences. The diocese had printed a thousand copies, to be given to those who visited the exhibition. Davide, when he saw the first printed copy, held it in his hands for ten minutes without saying a word. Then he took it to his mother, who worked nights as a nurse, and left it on the kitchen table, with a note: "For Rita. The first book by the son of the night."

Rita found it at seven in the morning, coming back from her night shift, tired as always. She sat down in the kitchen without taking off her coat and leafed through it all, page after page, while her coffee went cold. When she reached the last page, the one with the boy who asked too many questions, she saw that underneath there was a small dedication, handwritten: "To my mother, who keeps watch at night so that others can sleep. Like the painter who covered the face of sorrow." Rita cried silently for a quarter of an hour. Then, instead of going to bed, she went back to the hospital with the book under her arm and showed it to her colleagues on the day shift. That week the book passed from hand to hand throughout the ward. An elderly patient, an old carpenter from San Frediano, asked to keep it for a night. He returned it the next morning with a note: "I knew poplar. I made furniture from it for fifty years. I didn't know it kept a diary."

The opening was on a Saturday afternoon in mid-October. Everyone who had had anything to do with the Madonna came, and many others. Don Paolo came from San Leonardo with a coachload of parishioners, among them Signora Nunzia, who for the second time in a month was coming to Florence and said she had now got used to "city life". The bishop came with Monsignor Cappelli, who carried under his arm, as always, his calculator. Valeria came with her councillor's sash. Ferraris came from Milan, and this time too he paid for his ticket, even though entry was free: he left a euro in the church's offering box, which don Paolo had brought specially. Professor Ruggeri sent a bunch of flowers, because he was at a conference in Vienna, with a card: "To those who look carefully."

The speeches were short, at Chiara's insistence, as she had said clearly that people come to an exhibition to look, not to listen. The bishop thanked the parishioners, without whom the Madonna would never have reached Florence. Valeria thanked the cooperative, whose work, she said, had shown that a small neighbourhood workshop could do great things. Then Bellini was asked to say something, and he, who usually refused, accepted. He leaned on his stick and spoke for just one minute. "My grandfather Ernesto used to say that every painting has inside it the hands of the person who made it," he said. "Today in this room there are the hands of a fourteenth-century painter, of an eighteenth-century painter, of three restorers, of a boy who writes and of one who draws. And of a lady of ninety-two, who decided what to leave on top. Look at them all." Then he sat down, and the room applauded for a long time.

There was also someone nobody had invited. She was a very old lady, small, extremely elegant, with white hair gathered in a bun, a silver-topped stick and a pair of glasses as thick as the bottoms of bottles. She arrived alone, at five o'clock sharp, signed the visitors' book in a thin, old-fashioned hand, took a copy of Davide's book and stopped in front of the reconstruction of the fourteenth-century Madonna. She stayed there twenty minutes, without moving. Then she went up to Pietro's label, read it, took a magnifying glass out of her bag and went back to looking at the Madonna's hand, the one pointing down. Karl, who was watching her from a distance, suddenly recognised her and went pale. "Chiara," he whispered. "That's Professor Tolomei."

Elvira Tolomei was eighty-six and was, according to Karl, the greatest living expert on fourteenth-century Sienese painting. She had taught at the University of Siena for forty years, had written the Duccio catalogue on which every art historian in Italy had studied, and was said to recognise a painter's hand from a single centimetre of paint. Ruggeri himself had been her student, fifty years earlier. It was also said that she hadn't gone to exhibitions for years, because, she said, "today's exhibitions are made for people who don't look". Chiara went up to her, as nervous as a student at an exam. "Professor," she said, "it's an honour. Can I help you?" Professor Tolomei didn't turn round. She went on looking at the hand through the glass. "Yes," she said after a long moment. "Tell me who wrote this label."

Chiara called Pietro, who was explaining Davide's book to a group of parishioners. Pietro came over, saw the lady with the silver magnifying glass and, without knowing why, was afraid. Professor Tolomei lowered the glass and looked him up and down through her thick spectacles. "You wrote 'whoever looks carefully will perhaps find out'," she said. Pietro nodded. "It's a presumptuous sentence," she went on, and Pietro felt his cheeks burning. "But it's also true. I have been looking at Sienese paintings for seventy years, and I have seen that hand twice more in my life." She turned to the reconstruction and pointed with her silver stick at the Madonna's hand. "Once in a dispersed predella, which today is in a museum in Budapest. Another time in a fragment in the storerooms of the Pinacoteca in Siena, whose author nobody has ever identified."

Silence fell in the room. Chiara, Karl and Pietro looked at each other. Professor Tolomei sat down on one of the chairs set out for elderly visitors and asked for a glass of water. Then she explained, with the patience of someone who has taught for forty years, what she had seen. In fourteenth-century Sienese painting, she said, there were many Madonnas pointing at something, but they almost always pointed at the Child. It was a theological gesture: "Here is the way." This Madonna, on the other hand, pointed down, outside the picture, at a precise spot. It was a very rare gesture, which she had seen only in those two works. In both, under the Madonna, there had originally been a predella with portraits of the donors, kneeling, those who had paid for the painting. "The Madonna points at them," she said. "She presents them to the Child. Like a mother saying: look, it's them. Remember them."

Pietro felt his heart beating very hard. He asked, his voice trembling, whether the professor knew that, according to don Paolo, in the church floor, exactly at the spot indicated by the hand, there had been the tomb of the church's founders in the fourteenth century. Professor Tolomei looked at him for a long time. Then, for the first time since she had come in, she smiled. "No," she said. "I didn't know. Which makes everything much more interesting." She turned to don Paolo, who had come over with Signora Nunzia, and asked him whether the church kept any documents about its founders. Don Paolo replied that in the parish archive there was a parchment from 1327, which nobody had ever studied thoroughly, which spoke of a family of Sienese merchants who had "had the altar panel made for the souls of their dead".

"Thirteen twenty-seven," repeated Professor Tolomei, stressing each syllable. "Within the dendrochronology range." She stood up, leaning on her stick, with an energy nobody expected from a woman of eighty-six. "Father," she said to don Paolo, "on Monday I'm coming to San Leonardo. Have the parchment ready for me. And have this boy ready too." She pointed at Pietro with her stick. "Someone who writes such presumptuous labels must at least have the courage to verify them." Pietro couldn't say anything. Davide, who had heard everything from behind a panel, elbowed him so hard he almost fell over. "Did you see?" he whispered. "The hand. The hand was pointing at them. The dead." "Perhaps," replied Pietro, remembering Ruggeri. "It's compatible. Not proven." But he was smiling as he had never smiled before.

On Monday morning, in the parish house at San Leonardo, around the same wooden table on which the hypotheses had been formulated in June, Professor Tolomei read the 1327 parchment with her silver magnifying glass. It was written in Latin, in a tiny hand full of abbreviations. Pietro, Karl and don Paolo waited in silence. It took an hour. Then the professor looked up. The parchment was the will of a Sienese wool merchant, a certain Neri di Bindo, who left the church a sum of money so that "a panel with the Virgin showing her Son those who lie beneath her" should be painted, that is himself, his wife and their two children who had died of the plague. The painter's name was not there. But there was the description of the gesture, seven hundred years before anyone saw it again.

Pietro sat for a long time without saying anything. He thought of Signora Nunzia and the face of sorrow. He thought of a wool merchant who in 1327 had lost two children and had wanted a Madonna to point them out to the Child for ever. He thought of the eighteenth-century painter who, without knowing it, had covered that gesture out of pity. And he thought of Viola, of her question at Researchers' Night, of the promise written in the black notebook. "Professor," he said at last, "so the hand points at the dead. It's no longer a hypothesis." Professor Tolomei shook her head gently. "What we know," she said, "is that a man wanted a Madonna with that gesture, and that on that panel there is a Madonna with that gesture. It is very probable they are the same thing. But between 'very probable' and 'certain' lies the space in which historians work. And it's a very beautiful space. Don't be in a hurry to fill it."

Before leaving for Siena, Professor Tolomei did two things. The first was to ask Karl to send her the infrared photographs in high resolution: she wanted to compare them with the Budapest predella and the Pinacoteca fragment. "If the hand is the same," she said, "the Master of San Leonardo will have at least three works. Which, for an anonymous painter, is already a small career." The second was to take Pietro's pen and correct his label, which don Paolo had hung in the sacristy. She crossed out "What she is pointing at, nobody knows yet" and wrote above it, in her old-fashioned hand: "She points, in all probability, at the donors buried beneath the altar, according to the will of Neri di Bindo (1327)." Then she left the last sentence as it was. "Leave this one," she told Pietro, handing back the pen. "It's the only true thing one can say to those who come into a museum."

That evening Pietro went back to Florence and went straight up to the first floor, where Viola was having her bath. He sat on the edge of the tub, among the plastic ducks and the soap bubbles, and kept his promise. He told her about the wool merchant, his wife, the two dead children, the will. He explained that the Madonna's hand pointed at them, under the church floor, to tell the Child to remember them. Viola listened to everything with the utmost seriousness, a duck in her hand. Then she asked the question no art historian had ever asked. "And did the Child remember them?" Pietro didn't know what to answer. For the second time in a month, he said to Viola: "Good question. I don't know." Viola thought about it, then decided for herself. "Yes," she said. "Because the Madonna reminds him every day."

That same evening Pietro's phone rang. It was Professor Ruggeri, calling from Vienna, from his hotel room, who had just received an email from his old professor. "I hear Tolomei corrected one of your labels," he said without saying hello. Pietro, worried, said yes. There was a silence, then Ruggeri burst out laughing. "Do you know how many labels she corrected for me, when I was her student?" he said. "All of them. For two years. With a green pen, which was worse than the red one. And only once did she leave a sentence of mine as it was." Pietro asked which one. "I don't remember any more," Ruggeri admitted. "But I remember that on that day I decided to do this job." Then he became serious again. "The Master of the Hand," he said. "It's a fine name. We'll use it in the next article. And in the acknowledgements, once again, there'll be you. It's becoming a habit."

Ten days later an email arrived from Siena. It was written in perfect, old-fashioned Italian, without a single abbreviation, and began "Dear Mr Pietro". Professor Tolomei had compared Karl's photographs with the Budapest predella and the Pinacoteca fragment. The hand was the same: the same long fingers, the same way of painting the nails with a touch of white, the same bend of the wrist. "It follows," she wrote, "that the Master of San Leonardo is now the author of three works, which will have to be studied together. May I propose, for the catalogue I shall prepare, a more precise name: the Master of the Hand. Should you have no objection." At the bottom, after the signature, there was a postscript: "I hear from Ruggeri that you ask too many questions. Keep going. At my age, they are the only things still worth receiving."

In the black notebook, under the question mark as big as a page, Pietro finally wrote in red pen: "Verified (in all probability). The hand points at Neri di Bindo, his wife and their children, who died of the plague in 1327 or shortly before. Source: will, San Leonardo archive; reading by Prof. Tolomei." Then, below, he copied Viola's answer, word for word, because it seemed truer to him than all of his. And at the end, after thinking for a long time, he added a line for himself: "He who painted this Madonna has no name. But he has a hand. And whoever looks carefully sometimes discovers that a hand is enough." He reread the sentence and found it a little presumptuous. Then he remembered Professor Tolomei, smiled, and left it as it was.
